piece.title: String Quartet in E-flat major
piece.why: Fanny Hensel's Romanza: Violin I states the theme, the viola echoes a phrase, then the cello restates the theme in its high tenor register under a Violin I countermelody.

plan.summary: The tune starts in Violin 1 (bars 1–12). In bars 13–16 it moves down to the cello, and Violin 1 becomes a countermelody above it. In the cover, flute plays Violin 1 the whole way. Bassoon carries the bass line, alto sax and clarinet share the inner lines, and the sax takes the cello's tune in bars 13–16. In bar 1 the lowest note is actually the bottom of Violin 2's chord (G3), so the sax plays that bottom note there to keep the true bass underneath.

assignments.reason: Flute plays the Violin 1 line all the way through: the tune in bars 1–12, then the high countermelody. Every note (D4–D6) is in range, and flute handles the quick repeated eighths and the turns easily.
In bar 1 the bottom of Violin 2's chord (G3) is the lowest note in the texture, so the sax plays that bottom note to keep the real bass at the bottom, under the bassoon's B3s.
Violin 2 is the inner accompaniment, mostly repeated eighths, which the sax blends well with. Where Violin 2 has chords, the sax plays the top note.
Clarinet takes Violin 2 here (F4–G5) so the sax is free for the tune. Bar 13 is the phrase break, so the handover is natural.
Viola is the inner harmony. It goes down to D3, which only the clarinet can reach out of the free players. Its dark low register sounds like a viola.
In bars 13–16 the viola is the lowest part (long G3s, then D3), so the bassoon moves over to it and keeps the bass at the bottom.
Bassoon plays the cello bass line (E2–G4). It's all in range, including the moving eighth-note bass in bars 9–12.
The cello brings back the opening tune in the tenor register (C4–D5). Alto sax plays it at pitch because its warm, singing tone can carry the tune under the flute and clarinet.
